claim: Tuberculosis (TB) is a leading cause of death globally.
source: Tuberculosis (TB) is a leading cause of death globally.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific consensus about TB's global health impact.

claim: Of the 178/200 patients with persistent clonal infection >2 months, 27 developed new resistance mutations between sampling.
source: Of the 178/200 patients with persistent clonal infection >2 months, 27 developed new resistance mutations between sampling with 20/27 occurring in patients with pre-existing resistance.
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis of longitudinal isolate pairs from the study's patient cohort.

claim: 20/27 patients who developed new resistance mutations had pre-existing resistance.
source: Of the 178/200 patients with persistent clonal infection >2 months, 27 developed new resistance mutations between sampling with 20/27 occurring in patients with pre-existing resistance.
evidence: This is directly stated as a finding from the data analysis.

claim: Low abundance resistance variants at a purity of ≥19% in the first isolate predict fixation in the subsequent sample.
source: Low abundance resistance variants at a purity of ≥19% in the first isolate predict fixation in the subsequent sample.
evidence: This is a predictive finding based on analysis of allele frequency trajectories in the study data.

claim: The study identified significant in-host variation in 27 genes.
source: We identify significant in-host variation in 27 genes, including antibiotic resistance genes, metabolic genes and genes known to modulate host innate immunity and confirm several to be under positive selection by assessing phylogenetic convergence across a genetically diverse sample of 20,352 isolates.
evidence: This is a finding from the mutational density test and convergence analysis performed in the study.

claim: Only 5–10% of individuals infected with Mtbc develop active TB disease at some point in their lifetime.
source: Yet the majority of individuals exposed to Mtbc clear or contain the infection, and only 5–10% of those infected develop active TB disease at some point in their lifetime (Pai et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Pai et al., 2016.

claim: Attempts at effective vaccine development have repeatedly failed.
source: While basic human immune mechanisms to Mtbc have been identified, attempts at effective vaccine development guided by these mechanisms have repeatedly failed (Ernst, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ernst, 2018.

claim: Mtbc is an obligate human pathogen.
source: Mtbc is an obligate human pathogen (Gagneux, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Gagneux, 2018.

claim: All selective forces acting on Mtbc originate within the host.
source: Consequently, all selective forces acting on Mtbc will originate within the host, and the study of temporal dynamics of this is likely to inform antibiotic treatment (Sun et al., 2012) and rational vaccine design (Ernst, 2018).
evidence: This is an inference based on Mtbc being an obligate human pathogen, with citations supporting the implications.

claim: Infection consists of populations of Mtbc bacteria rather than single clones devoid of diversity.
source: The application of genome sequencing technologies to Mtbc isolates cultured from clinical samples has highlighted that infection consists of populations of Mtbc bacteria rather than single clones devoid of diversity (Copin et al., 2016; Didelot et al., 2016; Lieberman et al., 2014; Lieberman et al., 2011; Marvig et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior studies.

claim: Of the 307 patients with longitudinal samples collected, 32 patients had evidence for isolate microbiological contamination at any time point and were excluded.
source: Of the 307 patients with longitudinal samples collected (Supplementary file 1–2), 32 patients had evidence for isolate microbiological contamination at any time point (Goig et al., 2020) and were excluded.
evidence: This is a direct result from the quality control filtering process applied to the study data.

claim: 31 patients had evidence for mixed infection with two or more Mtbc lineages.
source: We found evidence for mixed infection with two or more Mtbc lineages (Wyllie et al., 2018) for 31 patients (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This is a finding from the F2 metric analysis shown in Figure 1B.

claim: 44 patients had evidence for re-infection with a different Mtbc strain between the first and second time points, using a pairwise genetic distance >7 fixed SNPs.
source: 44 patients had evidence for re-infection with a different Mtbc strain between the first and second time points, using a pairwise genetic distance >7 fixed SNPs (fSNPs) (Materials and methods, Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding based on the genetic distance threshold analysis shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The median fSNP distance for the 44 patients identified as reinfection was 708 (IQR 250–1086).
source: Median fSNP distance for the 44 patients identified as reinfection was 708 (IQR 250–1086).
evidence: This is a statistical summary of the genetic distance data for reinfection cases.

claim: 200 patients were identified as having persistent or relapsed clonal infection.
source: The remaining 200 patients were accordingly identified as having persistent or relapsed clonal infection (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is the final count after applying all exclusion criteria.

claim: The false error rate of the analysis pipeline for detecting allele frequency changes between sampling times was estimated at ≤0.053.
source: We estimated the false error rate of our analysis pipeline for detecting allele frequency changes between sampling times at ≤0.053 using a control dataset of 82 isolate pairs (162 total) that were in vitro technical or biological replicates (Materials and methods, Figure 4 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an estimate derived from analysis of technical replicate data.

claim: 1939 SNPs in antibiotic resistance loci changed in allele frequency by ≥5% across the sample of 200 patients.
source: We detected 1939 such SNPs across our sample of 200 patients (Figure 2B), 1774 were non-synonymous, 91 were intergenic, and 74 occurred within the rrs region (Supplementary file 6).
evidence: This is a count of SNPs meeting specific filtering criteria in the analysis.

claim: 1774 of the detected SNPs in antibiotic resistance loci were non-synonymous.
source: We detected 1939 such SNPs across our sample of 200 patients (Figure 2B), 1774 were non-synonymous, 91 were intergenic, and 74 occurred within the rrs region (Supplementary file 6).
evidence: This is a breakdown of SNP types from the data analysis.

claim: 11 cases of clonal interference were identified.
source: This identified 11 cases of clonal interference (Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1), demonstrating most often the fixation of a single allele in the second isolate from a mixture of multiple alleles at lower frequencies in the first isolate collected.
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of co-occurring resistance mutations with opposing allele frequency trajectories.

claim: Of the total 37 alleles that became fixed at the second time point, 10 had a frequency between 19% and 75% at the first time point.
source: Of the total 37 alleles that became fixed at the second time point, 10 (from seven patients) had a frequency between 19% and 75% at the first time point, two were detected at the first time point but had AF <19%, and the remaining majority, or 25, were undetectable (i.e. had support of <5 reads) at the first time point.
evidence: This is a breakdown of the allele frequency trajectories from the data analysis.

claim: 25 alleles that became fixed at the second time point were undetectable at the first time point.
source: Of the total 37 alleles that became fixed at the second time point, 10 (from seven patients) had a frequency between 19% and 75% at the first time point, two were detected at the first time point but had AF <19%, and the remaining majority, or 25, were undetectable (i.e. had support of <5 reads) at the first time point.
evidence: This is a finding from the allele frequency trajectory analysis.

claim: 27 AR SNPs were acquired in the 178 patients with persistent or relapsed clonal infection ≥2 months.
source: Twenty-seven AR SNPs were acquired in the 178 patients with persistent or relapsed clonal infection ≥2 months (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a count of resistance acquisition events from the data analysis.

claim: 9% (11/119) of patients with confirmed failure acquired ≥1 AR SNP.
source: Among the set of 119 patients with confirmed failure and known isolate sampling date, 9% (11/119) of these patients acquired ≥1 AR SNP.
evidence: This is a percentage calculated from the subset of patients with confirmed treatment failure.

claim: Of the 11 patients who acquired AR SNPs, 9 received fewer than four effective drugs.
source: Of the 11, 9 patients received fewer than four effective drugs.
evidence: This is a finding from the treatment regimen analysis.

claim: 259 pre-existing AR SNPs were identified with 41% (73/178) of failure patients harboring resistance to any drug at the first sampling.
source: Two hundred fifty-nine pre-existing AR SNPs were identified with 41% (73/178) of failure patients harboring resistance to any drug at the first sampling (Figure 3B, Supplementary file 7).
evidence: This is a count and percentage from the pre-existing resistance analysis.

claim: 64% (47/73) of patients with pre-existing resistance had MDR.
source: The majority of this resistance was MDR (multidrug resistance to at least isoniazid and a rifamycin), 64% (47/73) (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is a percentage calculated from the pre-existing resistance data.

claim: Five SNPs in glpK were detected among five replicate pairs (mean ΔAF = 45%).
source: We detected five SNPs in glpK (with ΔAF ≥ 25%) among five replicate pairs (mean ΔAF = 45%) consistent with an adaptive role for glpK mutations in vitro (Pethe et al., 2010; Vargas and Farhat, 2020) and accordingly excluded this gene from further analysis (Materials and methods).
evidence: This is a finding from the replicate pair analysis, with citations supporting the interpretation.

claim: The ΔAF threshold above which SNPs/isolate-pair were rare among technical replicates was determined to be 70%.
source: To clearly distinguish signal related to in-host factors from noise, we determined the ΔAF threshold above which SNPs/isolate-pair were rare among technical replicates that is, constituted 5% or less of total SNPs (Figure 4). We determined this ΔAF threshold to be 70%
evidence: This is a threshold determined from the distribution analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: 174 SNPs developed in-host among the 200 TB cases.
source: We determined this ΔAF threshold to be 70% and selected 174 SNPs that developed in-host (in-host SNPs) among the 200 TB cases (Figure 4C, Supplementary file 8).
evidence: This is a count of SNPs meeting the ΔAF threshold criterion.

claim: Of the 174 SNPs, 112 were non-synonymous, 42 synonymous, and 21 were intergenic.
source: Of the 174 SNPs, 112 were non-synonymous, 42 synonymous, and 21 were intergenic (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is a breakdown of SNP types from the annotation analysis.

claim: The 153/174 coding SNPs were distributed across 127/3,886 genes and were observed in 71/200 patients.
source: The 153/174 coding SNPs were distributed across 127/3,886 genes and were observed in 71/200 patients (Figure 5B and Figure 5D).
evidence: This is a summary of the distribution of coding SNPs across genes and patients.

claim: The GC > AT nucleotide transition was the most common mutation type.
source: We analyzed the spectrum of mutations and found the GC > AT nucleotide transition to be the most common.
evidence: This is a finding from the mutational spectrum analysis shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The transversion AT > TA was the least common substitution.
source: The transversion AT > TA was the least common substitution (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is a finding from the mutational spectrum analysis.

claim: Antibiotic resistance genes were on average the most diverse category while Essential genes varied the least.
source: Antibiotic resistance genes were on average the most diverse category while Essential genes varied the least (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is a finding from the nucleotide diversity analysis by gene category.

claim: Only one in-host SNP was detected within an epitope-encoding region in the gene PPE18.
source: Only one in-host SNP was detected within an epitope-encoding region in the gene PPE18 (Figure 6G and Figure 7—figure supplement 2, Supplementary file 12).
evidence: This is a finding from the epitope analysis.

claim: Three genes with unknown function (Rv0139, Rv0895, and Rv1543) were convergent in two patients each.
source: Three genes with unknown function: Rv0139, Rv0895, and Rv1543 were convergent in two patients each, two of which (Rv0139, Rv1543) had significant mutational density (p<2×10−5)
evidence: This is a finding from the convergence and mutational density analysis.

claim: Two genes (Rv0139, Rv1543) had significant mutational density (p<2×10−5).
source: Three genes with unknown function: Rv0139, Rv0895, and Rv1543 were convergent in two patients each, two of which (Rv0139, Rv1543) had significant mutational density (p<2×10−5)
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the mutational density test.

claim: PPE60 displayed significant mutational density (p<2×10−5).
source: three additional genes including PPE60 displayed significant mutational density (p<2×10−5) (Figure 5B, Supplementary file 13).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the mutational density test.

claim: Evidence for convergence was found in six pathways not known to result in antibiotic resistance.
source: We found evidence for convergence in six pathways not known to result in antibiotic resistance. These pathways are involved with biotin biosynthesis (fadD23, fadD29, and fadD30), ribosomal large subunit proteins (rpmB1, rplE, and rplY), glycerolipid and glycerophospholipid metabolism (aldA and Rv2974c), ESAT-6 protein secretion (eccCa1 and eccD1), coenzyme B12/cobalamin synthesis (cobH and cobK) and the uncharacterized pathway CBSS-164757.7.peg.5020 (fdxB and PPE18) (Supplementary file 17).
evidence: This is a finding from the pathway convergence analysis.

claim: 26/141 in-host SNPs were identified as phylogenetically convergent in the global sample of isolates.
source: We identified 26/141 in-host SNPs as phylogenetically convergent in our global sample of isolates (Supplementary file 19).
evidence: This is a finding from the phylogenetic convergence analysis using 20,352 global isolates.

claim: The convergent alleles included the PPE genes PPE18 (1 site), PPE54 (1 site) and PPE60 (3 sites).
source: The convergent alleles included the PPE genes PPE18 (1 site), PPE54 (1 site) and PPE60 (3 sites), as well as Rv0095c (2 sites) and Rv1944c (1 site) both conserved proteins of unknown function.
evidence: This is a finding from the phylogenetic convergence analysis.

claim: Rv0095c (2 sites) and Rv1944c (1 site) are convergent and are conserved proteins of unknown function.
source: The convergent alleles included the PPE genes PPE18 (1 site), PPE54 (1 site) and PPE60 (3 sites), as well as Rv0095c (2 sites) and Rv1944c (1 site) both conserved proteins of unknown function.
evidence: This is a finding from the phylogenetic convergence analysis.

claim: Convergent alleles were found in several antibiotic resistance loci: gyrB (1 site), gyrA (2 sites), rpoB (4 sites), rpoC (3 sites), inhA (1 site), embB (3 sites), and gid (1 site).
source: In addition to several SNPs in loci associated with antibiotic resistance, gyrB (1 site), gyrA (2 sites), rpoB (4 sites), rpoC (3 sites), inhA (1 site), embB (3 sites), and gid (1 site).
evidence: This is a finding from the phylogenetic convergence analysis.

claim: 9% of patients with confirmed delayed culture conversion, failure and relapse amplify resistance over time.
source: Here, we observe that 9% of patients with confirmed delayed culture conversion, failure and relapse amplify resistance over time.
evidence: This is a finding from the resistance acquisition analysis in the discussion.

claim: Sequencing revealed a substantial proportion of mixed infection or reinfection (28% of samples collected ≥2 months apart).
source: In addition to clonal acquisition of resistance, we find that sequencing revealed a substantial proportion of mixed infection or reinfection (28% of samples collected ≥2 months apart).
evidence: This is a percentage calculated from the exclusion analysis.

claim: The majority of alleles that sweep to fixation are not detectable at the first time point.
source: The low sensitivity is because the majority of alleles that sweep to fixation are actually not detectable at all at the first time point, suggesting that more frequent sampling may be needed.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the low sensitivity finding from the TPR/FPR analysis.

claim: Culturing sputa in vitro enriches Mtbc DNA for WGS but also creates experimental noise and can purge some of the genetic diversity present in the sputum sample.
source: While culturing sputa in vitro enriches Mtbc DNA for WGS it also creates experimental noise (Vargas and Farhat, 2020) and can purge some of the genetic diversity present in the sputum sample (Nimmo et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: The observed distribution of variants including the high rate of non-synonymous substitutions is consistent with the hypothesis of purifying pressure on synonymous variants.
source: The observed distribution of variants including the high rate of non-synonymous substitutions and the predominance of GC > AT variants are consistent with the hypotheses of purifying pressure on synonymous variants and oxidative DNA damage, respectively (Ford et al., 2011; Namouchi et al., 2012) in Mtbc.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data with citations to prior work supporting the hypothesis.

claim: The predominance of GC > AT variants is consistent with the hypothesis of oxidative DNA damage.
source: The observed distribution of variants including the high rate of non-synonymous substitutions and the predominance of GC > AT variants are consistent with the hypotheses of purifying pressure on synonymous variants and oxidative DNA damage, respectively (Ford et al., 2011; Namouchi et al., 2012) in Mtbc.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data with citations to prior work supporting the hypothesis.

claim: Host adaptive immunity does not drive directional selection in Mtbc genomes at short-time scales.
source: Overall, the observed diversity spared the CD4+ and CD8+ T cell epitope encoding regions of the genome providing further evidence that host adaptive immunity does not drive directional selection in Mtbc genomes now at short-time scales (Comas et al., 2010; Copin et al., 2014; Coscolla et al., 2015).
evidence: This is an inference from the epitope diversity analysis with citations to prior work.

claim: PPE genes may play an important role in the process of host-adaptation.
source: We found PPE genes to be more diverse in-host than PE genes and detected a signal of positive selection acting on three genes belonging to the PPE sub-family (Figure 7). This indicates that PPE genes may be play an important role in the process of host-adaptation.
evidence: This is an inference from the diversity and positive selection analysis.

claim: Mtbc is one of a few types of bacteria that possess the capacity for de novo coenzyme B12/cobalamin synthesis.
source: Mtbc is one of a few types of bacteria that possess the capacity for de novo coenzyme B12/cobalamin synthesis, and this pathway has been implicated in Mtbc survival in-host and Mtbc growth (Rowley and Kendall, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Rowley and Kendall, 2019.

claim: Four genetic variants developed in three separate patients and in three consecutive genes from the same locus cobG, intergenic cobG-cobH, cobH and cobK (Rv2064-Rv2067).
source: We identified four genetic variants that developed in three separate patients and in three consecutive genes from the same locus cobG, intergenic cobG-cobH, cobH and cobK (Rv2064-Rv2067).
evidence: This is a finding from the pathway convergence analysis.

claim: Biotin biosynthesis is relatively unique to mycobacteria and plays an important role in Mtbc growth, infection and host survival during latency.
source: Biotin biosynthesis is also relatively unique to mycobacteria and plays an important role in Mtbc growth, infection and host survival during latency (Salaemae et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Salaemae et al., 2011.

claim: ESAT-6 protein secretion is known to play a role in the modulation of host immune response by disrupting the phagosomal membrane.
source: The other identified pathways include ESAT-6 protein secretion known to play a role in the modulation of host immune response by disrupting the phagosomal membrane (Clemmensen et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Clemmensen et al., 2017.

claim: Rv0095c (SNP A85V) was recently associated with transmission success of an Mtbc cluster in Peru.
source: Although of unknown function, Rv0095c (SNP A85V) was recently associated with transmission success of an Mtbc cluster in Peru (Dixit et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Dixit et al., 2019.

claim: Both PPE18 and PPE60 have been shown to interact with toll-like receptor 2 (TLR2).
source: Both PPE18 and PPE60 have been shown to interact with toll-like receptor 2 (TLR2) (Nair et al., 2009; Su et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Nair et al., 2009 and Su et al., 2018.

claim: Mutations in the epitope-encoding regions of PPE18 have previously been described in a set of geographically separated clinical isolates.
source: PPE18 was the only gene to encode an epitope containing a SNP in-host; mutations in the epitope-encoding regions of this gene have previously been described in a set of geographically separated clinical isolates (Hebert et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Hebert et al., 2007.

claim: PPE18 codes for one of the antigens used in the construction of the M72/AS01E vaccine candidate.
source: Furthermore, PPE18 codes for one of the antigens used in the construction of the M72/AS01E vaccine candidate (Tait et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Tait et al., 2019.

claim: PPE54 has been implicated in Mtbc's ability to arrest macrophage phagosomal maturation (phagosome-lysosome fusion) and thought to be vital for intracellular persistence.
source: PPE54 has been implicated in Mtbc's ability to arrest macrophage phagosomal maturation (phagosome-lysosome fusion) and thought to be vital for intracellular persistence (Brodin et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Brodin et al., 2010.

claim: Mtbc modification of phagosomal function is thought to be TLR2/TLR4-dependent.
source: The mechanism by which PPE54 accomplishes this is unknown, but Mtbc modification of phagosomal function is thought to be TLR2/TLR4-dependent (Podinovskaia et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Podinovskaia et al., 2013.

claim: SNPs in human genes involved with innate-immune pathways have been implicated in host susceptibility to TB.
source: SNPs in human genes involved with innate-immune pathways have been implicated in-host susceptibility to TB (Azad et al., 2012; Kleinnijenhuis et al., 2011; Tientcheu et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: SNPs in TLR2 and TLR4 have been associated with susceptibility to TB disease.
source: Specifically, SNPs in TLR2 (thought to be the most important TLR in Mtbc recognition) (Tientcheu et al., 2017) and TLR4 have been associated with susceptibility to TB disease (Azad et al., 2012; Kleinnijenhuis et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: There is ongoing co-evolution between humans and Mtbc with evidence for reciprocal adaptive changes.
source: Taken together, these observations and our results are consistent with ongoing co-evolution between humans and Mtbc with evidence for reciprocal adaptive changes, leaving a signature of selection in both humans and Mtbc populations (Brites and Gagneux, 2015).
evidence: This is an inference from the combined observations with a citation supporting the co-evolution concept.

claim: Most co-evolution between Mtbc and humans is thought to have occurred long ago as a result of long-term host-pathogen interactions.
source: Most co-evolution between Mtbc and humans, the main reciprocal adaptations between host and pathogen are thought to have occurred long ago and as a result of long-term host-pathogen interactions (Azad et al., 2012; Brites and Gagneux, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The study included data for 614 clinical isolates of M. tuberculosis sampled from the sputum of 307 patients.
source: This study included data for 614 clinical isolates of M. tuberculosis that were sampled from the sputum of 307 patients resulting in n = 307 longitudinal pairs.
evidence: This is a description of the study sample size.

claim: The sequencing data for 456 publicly available isolates was downloaded from Genbank.
source: The sequencing data for 456 publicly available isolates was downloaded from Genbank (RRID:SCR_002760; Benson et al., 2009), sequenced using Illumina chemistry to generate paired-end reads and came from previously published studies (T [Trauner et al., 2017], C [Casali et al., 2016], W [Walker et al., 2013], B [Bryant et al., 2013], G [Guerra-Assunção et al., 2015], X [Xu et al., 2018], H [Witney et al., 2017], P [Farhat et al., 2019]; Figure 1—figure supplement 1, Supplementary file 1–2).
evidence: This describes the data sources with citations to the original studies.

claim: The study downloaded raw sequence data for 33,873 clinical isolates from the public domain.
source: We downloaded raw sequence data for 33,873 clinical isolates from the public domain (Benson et al., 2009).
evidence: This describes the global isolate dataset with a citation.

claim: CD4+ T and CD8+ T cell epitope sequences were downloaded from the Immune Epitope Database yielding a set of 2031 epitope sequences.
source: CD4+ T and CD8+ T cell epitope sequences were downloaded from the Immune Epitope Database (RRID: SCR_006604) (Vita et al., 2015) on May 23rd, 2018 according to criteria described previously (Coscolla et al., 2015) [linear peptides, M. tuberculosis complex (ID:77643, Mycobacterium complex), positive assays only, T cell assays, any MHC restriction, host: humans, any diseases, any reference type] yielding a set of 2031 epitope sequences (Supplementary file 11).
evidence: This describes the epitope data collection with citations.

claim: A final set of 1875 epitope sequences representing 348 genes (antigens) was used for downstream analysis.
source: We then filtered out any epitopes occurring in Mobile Genetic Elements which resulted in a final set of 1875 epitope sequences, representing 348 genes (antigens) used for downstream analysis.
evidence: This describes the final epitope dataset after filtering.

claim: There is a reduction in diversity at the second time point for patients in which drug-resistant alleles sweep to fixation.
source: Consistent with the idea that positive selection is acting on alleles within these loci, we observe a reduction in diversity at the second time point for the patients in which drug-resistant alleles sweep to fixation and in which putative host-pathogen alleles sweep to fixation (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is an observation from Figure 3A supporting the positive selection hypothesis.

claim: There is a reduction in diversity at the second time point for patients in which putative host-pathogen alleles sweep to fixation.
source: Consistent with the idea that positive selection is acting on alleles within these loci, we observe a reduction in diversity at the second time point for the patients in which drug-resistant alleles sweep to fixation and in which putative host-pathogen alleles sweep to fixation (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is an observation from Figure 3A supporting the positive selection hypothesis.

claim: The GC > AT transition is putatively due to oxidative damage including the deamination of cytosine/5-methyl-cytosine or the formation of 8-oxoguanine.
source: The GC > AT transition is putatively due to oxidative damage including the deamination of cytosine/5-methyl-cytosine or the formation of 8-oxoguanine (Dillon et al., 2015; Ford et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a mechanistic explanation supported by citations.

claim: Isolates from clonal infections spanned five of the eight known Mtbc lineages.
source: Isolates from these infections spanned five of the eight known Mtbc lineages (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is a description of the lineage distribution shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The coenzyme B12/cobalamin synthesis pathway has been implicated in Mtbc survival in-host and Mtbc growth.
source: Mtbc is one of a few types of bacteria that possess the capacity for de novo coenzyme B12/cobalamin synthesis, and this pathway has been implicated in Mtbc survival in-host and Mtbc growth (Rowley and Kendall, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Rowley and Kendall, 2019.

claim: Results demonstrating that PPE18 is under positive selection in the MTBC may have implications for the efficacy of the M72/AS01E vaccine against genetically diverse Mtbc strains.
source: Our results demonstrating that PPE18 is under positive selection in the MTBC may have implications for the efficacy of this vaccine against genetically diverse Mtbc strains.
evidence: This is a speculative inference about vaccine implications based on the positive selection finding.
